items.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007
items.q: When my Benny Goodman book came out, here is a white Jew, my editor recently departed, Sheldon Myer, regretfully, went to some of these people... said, “Look Jim treated Benny just the way he treated Louis and Duke.”

ctx.x: Fascinating. Tell me about playing jazz at Hamilton.

Well yeah, now there’s a lot to be said about all of that. If you read the jazz history books you do not understand that what was called Dixieland jazz, what we probably call classic jazz or trad jazz or something of that kind, was the most popular form of jazz in the United States. You had, beginning in around 1936, you began to have the so-called Dixieland revival. And I won’t go into all the detail of that because it’d take too long. But you began having these bands, people as a result of the swing boom there…

guys and bringing them out. And around the northeast it was more the Condon group with the Wild Bill Davison with George Brunies, Pee Wee Russell and Hall, Bobby Hackett, Teagarden, you know, those names. And so by the late thirties, early forties, if you were interested in jazz it was this, it was Dixieland jazz, or whatever term you want to use. And you began to score in the swing bands. Now Benny Goodman, aww come on, that’s swing. It was these Condon bands or the Lu Watters band or Bunk Johnson or whatever it…
